newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-HENMAN ANSWERS A NATION'S PRAYERS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HENMAN ANSWERS A NATION'S PRAYERS.

text.p: An American journalist nudged his colleague as Tim Henman stood on Centre Court, match point down to Paul Haarhuis in the fifth set of Wimbledon's most epic match of the year.

"Say," he snorted, "Too bad the Brits are going to lose Hong Kong and Henman at the same time." The sun may indeed be setting on one corner of the empire, but in south-west London they are made of sterner stuff.
Henman's remarkable 6-7 6-3 6-2 4-6 14-12 victory produced the sort of theatre which individual British sportsmen rarely experience even on home soil.

In normal circumstances, the 22-year-old from Oxford could have expected to provoke a reaction somewhere between polite delight and enthusiastic cheering, but on Sunday he reaped unexpected benefit from the dismal weather which brought the tournament almost to its knees in the first week.

Forced to throw open their doors on the middle Sunday for only the second time in their history, the All England Club found themselves hosting the most partisan crowd ever found at this most traditional of venues.
Even before Henman appeared, the Mexican waves had begun and his arrival on court was greeted with the sort of rapture normally afforded Princess Diana by evening gown salesmen.

What subsequently unfolded around him during a contest which spanned almost four hours was so untypically British that Haarhuis might have imagined himself at a packed Foro Italico or facing Jimmy Connors at night at Flushing Meadow.

They booed the Dutchman's double faults, they howled at his mishits and any flashing Henman winners induced total pandemonium. When Haarhuis double faulted on match point at 5-4 in the fifth set, they probably heard the roar in Beijing.

"From the word go it was something I haven't experienced before," admitted Henman, remarkably calm for a man who had sparked the drama by wasting six set points in the first set, three of them double faults.

"I didn't hear a ball being hit in the knock-up, there was so much noise. I always go on court to play for myself, but I realised at that point I couldn't have greater support. Every time I won a point I thought the roof would come off. I'm sure they played a great part in the match.

"It's very difficult to put into words but it gives you an amazing buzz to hear all of them singing your name. I'd love exactly the same crowd to be watching when I play Richard Krajicek in the next round."

The gentlemanly Haarhuis, who experienced the lonely experience of playing Connors in front of a baying New York crowd in the quarter-finals of the 1991 U.S. Open, deserved huge credit for keeping his cool on court but sidestepped questions about whether the crowd had strayed beyond acceptable boundaries.
"That's too difficult," he said. "But the crowd didn't make me lose the match. It might make him play better but it doesn't affect me."
Henman's fourth round showdown with Krajicek, the defending champion and the only other seed left in the bottom half of the draw, will now grip the attention for a variety of reasons.

Can Britain, who last produced a Wimbledon men's champion in 1936, end a drought which looked irreversible even three years ago? Can Henman again confound those who insist he has too few major weapons to win on grass? Can fellow Briton Greg Rusedski join him in the quarter-finals? And, most intriguing of all, how will the atmosphere compare when the regular Centre Court crowd of debenture-holders and ballot winners are restored to their seats?
'Henmania' is now so deeply entrenched anything is possible but the object of all the interest is hopeful his new-found army of soccer-style supporters will return.

"I've never played at Wembley, but I can say that's as good as it gets in tennis," admitted Henman. "Unfortunately, I don't think a lot of them will be there for my next match. But I'll just approach it concentrating on my own game and firmly believing I can win."
Among the many ironies of the day was that Henman's marathon delayed the transmission of the BBC's "Songs of Praise" programme, pre-recorded at the All England Club's new Number One court.
By the time it went on air, a nation's prayers had already been answered.
